project_name: Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems
initial_requirements: The Ministry of Home Affairs needs a Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems application to improve day-to-day police work and support better crime investigation and criminal detection. The system will be used by investigating officers, records staff, and citizens. It should provide an initial foundation for registering complaints, supporting investigations, and exchanging relevant information between police units and the public.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What are the primary outcomes and success criteria the Ministry wants this Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems application to achieve in its first release for police officers, records staff, and citizens?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
In the first release, we want officers to be able to register complaints and start case tracking much faster, with less manual paperwork and fewer delays in sharing information between units. For records staff, the success is having a single place to capture, search, and retrieve complaint and case details reliably, so they can support investigations without re-entering the same data again and again.
For citizens, the main outcome is easier complaint submission and better visibility that their complaint has been received and is being handled. We would consider it successful if the system is actually used in day-to-day police work, reduces turnaround time for basic registration and lookup tasks, and improves coordination between police staff and the public.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Through which channels should citizens be able to submit complaints in the first release—for example, in person at a police station, online web portal, mobile app, phone-assisted entry, or other channels—and are any channels required to be prioritized or excluded?
turns.interviewee_utterance: For the first release, I would expect in-person submission at the police station to be mandatory, because that matches current practice and helps us ensure no one is left out. An online web portal would also be important so citizens can file complaints without visiting the station, but I’m not sure about a mobile app yet, and phone-assisted entry may be more of a later enhancement unless the team decides it’s needed for accessibility. I don’t think we should exclude any existing channel at this stage, but the priority would likely be station-based entry first, then web submission.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What are the key business rules and case lifecycle states we should enforce in the first release—for example, how a complaint moves from submission to review, investigation, closure, or escalation, and what conditions determine each transition?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
In the first release, a complaint should start as submitted or registered, then move to under review once a records officer or duty officer checks it for completeness and urgency. If it is valid and actionable, it should become assigned or under investigation when handed to an investigating officer, and then move to closed when the case is resolved, or escalated if it needs a higher unit, another jurisdiction, or a specialized team.
The main condition for each transition is basically authorization and case validity: incomplete or duplicate complaints may need clarification before moving forward, urgent matters should be marked for immediate attention, and closure should only happen after the investigation outcome is recorded. If a complaint turns out to be outside police scope or needs transfer, it should not just disappear; it should be formally rejected, referred, or escalated with a reason captured.

turns.interviewer_utterance: For complaints submitted in person at the police station and later through the web portal, how should the system verify a citizen’s identity or authenticity of the complaint in the first release, and what specific proof or checks should be required?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
For in-person complaints, I would expect the officer or records staff to verify identity using some government-issued ID and capture the complainant’s basic details against that document. For web portal submissions, we should at least require the citizen to create an account or use a verified login, plus provide contact details so the complaint can be traced back if needed.
I’m not sure we need very heavy proof in the first release beyond that, unless the complaint is very sensitive or high-risk. If the team wants stricter checks, we could require an OTP to the registered phone or email and maybe supporting documents to be uploaded when available, but that would need to be confirmed with the police side.

turns.interviewer_utterance: When officers or records staff review a submitted complaint, what exact rules should the system use to determine whether it is complete, valid, duplicate, or otherwise not actionable, and how should it detect and handle possible duplicates across existing complaints or cases?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
A complaint should be treated as complete if it has the basic identity details of the complainant, a clear description of the incident, date or approximate time, location, and enough information to understand what happened. It would be valid if it is within police scope and has enough facts to start an entry; if key details are missing, the system should mark it as incomplete and send it back for clarification rather than pushing it into investigation.
For duplicates, the system should compare things like complainant name or contact, incident date, location, and a summary of the allegation against existing complaints and open cases. If there is a likely match, it should flag it for human review instead of auto-closing it, because two complaints can look similar but still be separate incidents; only after review should staff merge, link, or mark it as a duplicate with a reason.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What roles and permission boundaries should the first release enforce for officers, records staff, and citizens—for example, who can create, view, edit, assign, escalate, close, or search complaints and case records, and what information should each role be prevented from seeing or changing?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
Citizens should only be able to create their own complaints, view the status of their own submissions, and add any follow-up information that is requested or allowed. They should not be able to see internal notes, officer assignments, investigation details, or other citizens’ records.
Records staff should be able to create and search complaints, verify completeness, update basic registration details, and route cases, but they should not close investigations or alter substantive case findings. Investigating officers should be able to view and update assigned cases, add investigation notes, escalate when needed, and close cases when appropriate, while access to sensitive records should be limited by role and, if necessary, by station or jurisdiction.

turns.interviewer_utterance: You mentioned that some sensitive records may need to be limited by station or jurisdiction as well as by role. Could you describe the exact access rules you want for cases across stations and jurisdictions—for example, who can view, edit, transfer, or share a complaint or case when it belongs to another station, and what conditions must be met for cross-station access or escalation?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
Yes, the general rule should be that a station can fully work only on its own registered cases unless there is an approved transfer or escalation. Officers or staff from another station should not edit a case from outside their jurisdiction unless they are formally assigned, asked to assist, or the case has been escalated to them by an authorized supervisor.
Cross-station access should be allowed for viewing only when there is a legitimate operational need and the user has the right role, but any transfer or sharing should leave an audit trail and mention the reason, since jurisdiction matters a lot. If a complaint belongs to another area, the system should let it be referred or escalated rather than copied around freely, and only supervisors or designated administrators should approve those movements.

slots.name: project_goals
slots.value: Enable faster complaint registration and case tracking, reduce manual paperwork and delays in sharing information between units, provide a single reliable place to capture/search/retrieve complaint and case details, and improve citizen complaint submission and visibility; success is measured by day-to-day use, reduced turnaround time, and better coordination between police staff and the public.

slots.value: Investigating officers, records staff, and citizens.

slots.name: functional_needs

slots.name: business_rules

Complaints may be escalated for higher units, other jurisdictions, or specialized teams, or formally rejected/referred with a reason if outside police scope. Incomplete, duplicate, or otherwise invalid complaints require clarification before progression; urgent matters should be marked for immediate attention.

slots.value: Cross-station viewing is allowed only for legitimate operational need and proper role; any sharing, transfer, or escalation must be authorized, reasoned, and audited.

abduction_history.surprising_fact: The stakeholder explicitly prefers in-person station-based complaint submission as mandatory for the first release, despite also wanting an online portal soon after.
abduction_history.suspected_reason: This likely reflects a need to preserve equitable access and trusted verification in the initial rollout, while reducing risk around identity validation, complaint authenticity, and excluding citizens who may not have reliable internet access or digital literacy.

abduction_history.surprising_fact: The stakeholder wants complaints that are incomplete, duplicate, or outside police scope to be held for clarification, rejected, referred, or escalated with reasons, rather than simply closed or discarded.
abduction_history.suspected_reason: This suggests the Ministry likely needs strong accountability and traceability so no citizen complaint is lost, misclassified, or informally dropped, and so supervisors can audit why a case did not proceed through the normal investigation path.

abduction_history.surprising_fact: The initial requirements emphasize faster registration and centralized tracking, but they do not yet mention how officers, records staff, and citizens will be authenticated or authorized to access different complaint and case functions, even though the system will handle sensitive crime data and may expose different views through station entry and a web portal.
abduction_history.suspected_reason: This likely reflects an implicit need for role-based control and accountability: the Ministry may need to ensure that sensitive case information is only visible or editable by the right police personnel, while citizens can only access their own submissions and limited status updates.

abduction_history.surprising_fact: The stakeholder says sensitive records may need to be limited not only by role but also by station or jurisdiction, which introduces an additional access-control boundary beyond the basic officer/records/citizen roles.
abduction_history.suspected_reason: This likely reflects a federated policing structure where cases and records are operationally owned by specific stations or jurisdictions, so the Ministry needs to prevent unauthorized cross-station access while still allowing controlled sharing for escalations and transfers.

abduction_history.surprising_fact: The stakeholder emphasized that in-person station-based submission is mandatory for the first release, but also wants to prioritize a web portal soon after and has not yet confirmed whether phone-assisted entry or mobile access should be supported.
abduction_history.suspected_reason: This suggests the Ministry is balancing equitable access and trusted identity verification against rollout risk, while also anticipating that some citizens may have limited internet access, low digital literacy, or accessibility needs that could affect how complaints are submitted in practice.
